claim: N6-methyladenosine is the most prominent RNA modification in mammals.
source: N6-methyladenosine is the most prominent RNA modification in mammals.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about m6A prevalence in mammals.

claim: m6A loss profoundly alters cellular fate choices and tissue architecture in all skin lineages.
source: Tapping physiological relevance, we show that m6A loss profoundly alters these cues and perturbs cellular fate choices and tissue architecture in all skin lineages.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the conditional knockout studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: There is a correlation between m6A modification in coding sequences and enhanced translation.
source: Contrasting with in vivo ribosomal profiling, we unearth a correlation between m6A modification in coding sequences and enhanced translation, particularly of key morphogenetic signaling pathways.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of miCLIP data with ribosomal profiling data shown in the manuscript.

claim: Signaling and canonical translation pathways show significant downregulation after m6A loss.
source: By single-cell transcriptomics and bioinformatics, both signaling and canonical translation pathways show significant downregulation after m6A loss.
evidence: This is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data and bioinformatics analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Many highly m6A-modified mRNAs are markedly upregulated upon m6A loss.
source: Interestingly, however, many highly m6A-modified mRNAs are markedly upregulated upon m6A loss, and they encode RNA-methylation, RNA-processing and RNA-metabolism factors.
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data comparing control and Mettl3 cKO samples.

claim: m6A functions to enhance translation of key morphogenetic regulators.
source: Together, our findings suggest that m6A functions to enhance translation of key morphogenetic regulators, while also destabilizing sentinel mRNAs that are primed to activate rescue pathways when m6A levels drop.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the combined miCLIP, ribosomal profiling, and loss-of-function data.

claim: m6A destabilizes sentinel mRNAs that are primed to activate rescue pathways when m6A levels drop.
source: Together, our findings suggest that m6A functions to enhance translation of key morphogenetic regulators, while also destabilizing sentinel mRNAs that are primed to activate rescue pathways when m6A levels drop.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that highly m6A-modified mRNAs encoding RNA metabolism factors are upregulated upon m6A loss.

claim: m6A is the most abundant modification on mRNAs.
source: Among the over 100 types of RNA modifications identified thus far, m6A is the most abundant modification on mRNAs.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction.

claim: Previous studies have identified m6A methyltransferases (writers), m6A demethylases (erasers) and factors that recognize m6A-modified RNAs (readers).
source: Previous studies have identified m6A methyltransferases (writers), m6A demethylases (erasers) and also factors that recognize m6A-modified RNAs (readers) (Alarcón et al., 2015; Bokar et al., 1997; Liu et al., 2014; Meyer et al., 2015; Meyer and Jaffrey, 2017; Patil et al., 2016; Zheng et al., 2013; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: m6A can exert context-dependent effects on distinct steps of RNA metabolism.
source: Finally, m6A can exert context-dependent effects on distinct steps of RNA metabolism, compounding the unpredictability of whether a modification will impart to a given target increased or decreased expression.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on prior literature and the complexity observed in various studies.

claim: Embryonic skin epithelium begins as a single layer of multipotent epithelial progenitors.
source: Embryonic skin epithelium begins as a single layer of multipotent epithelial progenitors, which will develop into three strikingly distinct tissues: epidermis, hair follicles (HFs) and sebaceous glands (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about skin development, illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: WNT signaling plays a critical role in specifying the HF fate.
source: WNTs play a critical role in specifying the HF fate (Andl et al., 2002; Gat et al., 1998; van Genderen et al., 1994; Huelsken et al., 2001; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: WNThi embryonic progenitors cluster into hair placodes.
source: Within the basal epidermal plane, WNThi embryonic progenitors cluster into hair placodes (Ahtiainen et al., 2016), which emerge in three waves beginning at embryonic day 14.5 (E14.5) and develop into fully mature HFs by birth (Duverger and Morasso, 2009; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Hair placodes emerge in three waves beginning at embryonic day 14.5 (E14.5) and develop into fully mature HFs by birth.
source: Within the basal epidermal plane, WNThi embryonic progenitors cluster into hair placodes (Ahtiainen et al., 2016), which emerge in three waves beginning at embryonic day 14.5 (E14.5) and develop into fully mature HFs by birth (Duverger and Morasso, 2009; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The first divisions in WNThi placode cells are asymmetric, generating WNTlo daughters that will give rise to hair follicle stem cells (HFSCs) and outer root sheath, and WNThi daughters that will generate the inner root sheath and hair shaft of the follicles.
source: The first divisions in WNThi placode cells are asymmetric, generating WNTlo daughters that will give rise to hair follicle stem cells (HFSCs) and outer root sheath, and WNThi daughters that will generate the inner root sheath and hair shaft of the follicles (Ouspenskaia et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Sebaceous glands spawn from the upper portion of each HF near birth.
source: Near birth, oil-rich sebaceous glands spawn from the upper portion of each HF (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about skin development, illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Sebaceous gland development is favored over HFs in mice whose skin expresses ΔNLEF1, a dominant-negative disrupter of WNT signaling.
source: Sebaceous gland development is favored over HFs in mice whose skin expresses ΔNLEF1, a dominant-negative disrupter of WNT signaling (Merrill et al., 2001; Niemann et al., 2003), indicating that WNT levels play an important role in balancing these fate choices.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: WNT levels play an important role in balancing fate choices between sebaceous glands and HFs.
source: Sebaceous gland development is favored over HFs in mice whose skin expresses ΔNLEF1, a dominant-negative disrupter of WNT signaling (Merrill et al., 2001; Niemann et al., 2003), indicating that WNT levels play an important role in balancing these fate choices.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies on ΔNLEF1 expression.

claim: Lower levels of WNT signaling favor epidermal over HF fates.
source: Lower levels of WNT signaling also favor epidermal over HF fates, as in the developing plane of embryonic progenitors, those with lower levels of WNT signaling become fated to become epidermal progenitors, which fuel the production of upward columns of terminally differentiated cells that form the skin's barrier that excludes pathogens and retains body fluids.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the role of WNT signaling in skin fate determination.

claim: Epidermal differentiation is regulated by NOTCH signaling and MYC activation.
source: This differentiation program is regulated by NOTCH signaling and MYC activation (Blanpain et al., 2006; Frye et al., 2003; Gandarillas and Watt, 1997; Moriyama et al., 2008; Rangarajan et al., 2001; Watt et al., 2008a; Watt et al., 2008b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Skin progenitors maintain reduced levels of protein synthesis relative to their differentiating progeny.
source: Similar to the hematopoietic system (Buszczak et al., 2014; Signer et al., 2014), skin progenitors maintain reduced levels of protein synthesis relative to their differentiating progeny (Blanco et al., 2016; Liakath-Ali et al., 2018; Sendoel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In differentiating skin cells, 5-methylcytosine (m5C) is enhanced, which protects tRNAs from cleavage and facilitates protein translation.
source: In differentiating skin cells, 5-methylcytosine (m5C) is enhanced, which protects tRNAs from cleavage and facilitates protein translation (Blanco et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Under conditions of stress in the epidermis, EIF2α is phosphorylated, dampening protein translation.
source: Under conditions of stress in the epidermis, EIF2α is phosphorylated, dampening protein translation, while a less efficient, more promiscuous initiator, EIF2A, translates key proteins that allow progenitor survival in a harsher environment (Sendoel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: When translational control is compromised in the skin, epidermal, HF and sebaceous gland stem cell compartments respond differently.
source: Interestingly, however, when translational control is compromised in the skin, epidermal, HF and sebaceous gland stem cell compartments respond differently, with epidermal cells implementing a feedback mechanism to increase global translation (Liakath-Ali et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: 157,641 m6A sites were identified within 11,420 transcripts in P0 skin progenitors.
source: Based upon the crosslinking-induced mutations detected in the miCLIP libraries, 11,420 transcripts displayed a total of 157,641 sites that were modified by m6A and typified by a 'DRACH' motif (Fu et al., 2014; Linder et al., 2015; Figure 1D; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by the miCLIP experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: m6A sites are typified by a 'DRACH' motif.
source: Based upon the crosslinking-induced mutations detected in the miCLIP libraries, 11,420 transcripts displayed a total of 157,641 sites that were modified by m6A and typified by a 'DRACH' motif (Fu et al., 2014; Linder et al., 2015; Figure 1D; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by the miCLIP data and prior literature on m6A motifs.

claim: m6A density was highest around mRNA stop codons.
source: The data were highly reproducible across three independent replicates, and as previously noted, m6A density was highest around mRNA stop codons (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the miCLIP data shown in Figure 1E and is consistent with prior knowledge.

claim: mRNAs with high levels of m6A modification tended to be more highly translated than those with low modification.
source: Intriguingly, mRNAs with high levels of m6A modification tended to be more highly translated than those with low modification (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of miCLIP and ribosomal profiling data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The correlation between m6A modification and translation efficiency was most striking when focusing on m6A modifications in the coding sequence.
source: This correlation was most striking when we focused on m6A modifications in the coding sequence.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis of miCLIP and ribosomal profiling data presented in Figure 1F.

claim: GSEA of m6A-modified mRNAs featured 'basal cell carcinoma', dominated by WNT and SHH signaling factors, and 'NOTCH signaling' among the top three categories.
source: Gene set enrichment analyses (GSEA) upon that value featured 'basal cell carcinoma', dominated by WNT and SHH signaling factors, and 'NOTCH signaling' among the top three categories (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis of the miCLIP data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: The top three GSEA categories tended to be more efficiently translated than other pathways.
source: Interestingly, these top three categories tended to be more efficiently translated than other pathways (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of translation efficiency data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The top categories of highly m6A-modified and highly translated mRNAs were signaling pathways including ECM-receptor interactions, basal cell carcinoma (dominated by mRNAs encoding WNT and SHH signaling factors) and NOTCH signaling.
source: The top categories sharing these criteria were signaling pathways including ECM-receptor interactions, basal cell carcinoma (dominated by mRNAs encoding WNT and SHH signaling factors) and NOTCH signaling (Figure 1G; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: WNT signaling, SHH signaling, and NOTCH signaling pathways play essential roles in HF morphogenesis.
source: These pathways play essential roles in HF morphogenesis (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is established knowledge about HF development, illustrated in Figure 1H.

claim: WNT signaling precedes SHH signaling in hair follicle development.
source: Notably, WNT signaling, which prompts basal progenitors to organize into hair placodes, precedes SHH signaling (Woo et al., 2012), and WNT signaling is required to maintain SHH pathway-driven basal cell carcinomas in mice and in humans (Sánchez-Danés et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: WNT signaling is required to maintain SHH pathway-driven basal cell carcinomas in mice and in humans.
source: Notably, WNT signaling, which prompts basal progenitors to organize into hair placodes, precedes SHH signaling (Woo et al., 2012), and WNT signaling is required to maintain SHH pathway-driven basal cell carcinomas in mice and in humans (Sánchez-Danés et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The METTL3-METTL14 writer complex is responsible for adding the vast majority of m6A onto RNAs.
source: The METTL3-METTL14 writer complex is responsible for adding the vast majority of m6A onto RNAs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations in the introduction.

claim: Upon ablation of Mettl3 or Mettl14, global m6A is dramatically diminished in a wide variety of cell types.
source: Upon ablation of Mettl3 or Mettl14, global m6A is dramatically diminished in a wide variety of cell types (Batista et al., 2014; Cheng et al., 2019; Cui et al., 2017; Geula et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2014; Vu et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2014b; Weng et al., 2018; Yao et al., 2018; Yoon et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Krt14-Cre is active exclusively in the epidermal progenitors beginning at E13.5.
source: Active exclusively in the epidermal progenitors beginning at E13.5 (Vasioukhin et al., 1999), Krt14-Cre had excised the stop codon in the Rosa26 locus by E14.5 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: By E16.5, expression of METTL3 was largely abolished within the targeted YFP+ cells in the cKO skin epithelium.
source: Whole-mount immunofluorescence imaging revealed that by E16.5, expression of METTL3 was largely abolished within the targeted YFP+ cells in the cKO skin epithelium (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: METTL3 was predominantly nuclear in control epithelial progenitors.
source: And consistent with its known location in other cell types (Kwon et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2014; Schöller et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018), METTL3 was predominantly nuclear in control (Ctrl) epithelial progenitors.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data and citations to prior literature.

claim: One allele of Mettl3 was enough to sustain a normal m6A level on mRNAs.
source: Quantification of the m6A/A ratio based on the radioactive signals revealed a comparable m6A content on mRNAs from wild-type Mettl3+/+ and heterozygous Mettl3+/- cells, indicating that one allele of Mettl3 was enough to sustain a normal m6A level on mRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by TLC data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Throughout embryogenesis, control and cKO mice were grossly comparable in appearance.
source: Throughout embryogenesis, control and cKO mice were grossly comparable in appearance (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by images shown in Figure 2D.

claim: From postnatal day 2 (P2) onward, phenotypic abnormalities of the cKO animals began to emerge.
source: From postnatal day 2 (P2) onward, however, phenotypic abnormalities of the cKO animals began to emerge.
evidence: This is supported by observations and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Most striking was the progressive decline in body sizes and weights of cKO animals compared to their control littermates.
source: Most striking was the progressive decline in body sizes and weights compared to their control littermates (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Most cKO animals did not survive beyond postnatal day 6 (P6).
source: Most cKO animals did not survive beyond postnatal day 6 (P6).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: No significant TEWL differences were observed between control and cKO skin, ruling against dehydration as a cause of death.
source: To investigate potential causes of the lethality, we assessed the epidermal barrier function by measuring the trans-epidermal water loss (TEWL) rate of the control and cKO skin at P0 and P6. No significant TEWL differences were observed, ruling against dehydration as a cause of death (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by TEWL measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Tongue filiform papillae, necessary for suckling and food intake, were notably diminished in cKO animals.
source: Examination of oral tissues indicated that both teeth and tongue formed, but tongue filiform papillae, necessary for suckling and food intake at this stage, were notably diminished (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D,E.

claim: Back skin HF morphogenesis was severely altered in the cKO animals.
source: Back skin HF morphogenesis was also severely altered in the cKO animals.
evidence: This is supported by multiple lines of evidence including histology and immunofluorescence data.

claim: The numbers of de novo placodes began to decline soon after Mettl3 ablation.
source: This began to surface soon after Mettl3 ablation where the numbers of de novo placodes began to decline, and progressed thereafter as judged by the paucity of hair germs and pegs at birth (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: With the exception of the sparse, large guard hairs, which form prior to Krt14-Cre activity and do not use WNT signaling in their specification, HF downgrowth was largely impaired and HFs failed to mature beyond the peg stage.
source: Analyses of the few pups still alive by P6 revealed that with the exception of the sparse, large guard hairs, which form prior to Krt14-Cre activity and do not use WNT signaling in their specification, HF downgrowth was largely impaired and HFs failed to mature beyond the peg stage (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2F.

claim: The defects did not appear to reflect developmental delays, but rather altered morphogenesis.
source: Based upon these data, the defects did not appear to reflect developmental delays, but rather altered morphogenesis.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the temporal analysis of the phenotypes.

claim: At E17.5, nuclear LEF1 was significantly diminished in the basal (placode) progenitors within the epidermal plane as well as WNThi cells in the developing HFs of cKO skin.
source: Immunofluorescence revealed that at E17.5, nuclear LEF1 was significantly diminished in the basal (placode) progenitors within the epidermal plane as well as WNThi cells in the developing HFs of cKO skin (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in Figure 3A.

claim: At P0, LEF1 levels remained low in the WNThi cells and were also diminished in the underlying dermal condensates.
source: At P0, LEF1 levels remained low in the WNThi cells. It was also diminished in the underlying dermal condensates (precursors to the dermal papilla, DP), whose WNT signaling and nuclear LEF1 is known to be dependent upon epithelial WNT signaling (Mok et al., 2019; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B and a citation to prior literature.

claim: In Mettl3 null HFs, β-catenin was mostly at the intercellular borders, reflective of its WNT-independent role at adherens junctions.
source: Notably, immunohistochemistry revealed that in contrast to control HFs, which showed appreciable anti-β-catenin nuclear staining at the follicle:DP interface, in Mettl3 null HFs, β-catenin was mostly at the intercellular borders, reflective of its WNT-independent role at adherens junctions (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Mettl3 null HF progenitors were perturbed in engulfing the DP, a feature seen when WNT signaling and/or SHH signaling are inhibited.
source: Additionally, these HF progenitors were perturbed in engulfing the DP, a feature seen when WNT signaling and/or SHH signaling are inhibited (Heitman et al., 2020; Matos et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by observations and citations to prior literature.

claim: While SHH signaling was not blocked in the absence of METTL3, it was aberrant, with an overall reduction, particularly in the epithelium.
source: Since SHH signaling is dependent upon WNT signaling, we next tested for the activation of this pathway. To do so, we mated our mice to Gli1-lacZ mice, and performed X-gal histochemical staining on skin sections. While SHH signaling was not blocked in the absence of METTL3, it was aberrant, with an overall reduction, particularly in the epithelium (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by X-gal staining data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Laminin 5-1-1 is required for HF downgrowth and SHH signaling.
source: These results were intriguing in light of the knowledge that laminin 5-1-1 is required for HF downgrowth and SHH signaling (Fleger-Weckmann et al., 2016; Gao et al., 2008), and that Lama5 and Lamac1 were among the most highly modified and efficiently translated mRNAs in skin (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Lama5 and Lamac1 were among the most highly modified and efficiently translated mRNAs in skin.
source: These results were intriguing in light of the knowledge that laminin 5-1-1 is required for HF downgrowth and SHH signaling (Fleger-Weckmann et al., 2016; Gao et al., 2008), and that Lama5 and Lamac1 were among the most highly modified and efficiently translated mRNAs in skin (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by the miCLIP and ribosomal profiling data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Sebaceous glands use a different hedgehog pathway and require reduced WNT signaling for their formation.
source: As an appendage of HFs, sebaceous glands use a different hedgehog pathway and require reduced WNT signaling for their formation (Merrill et al., 2001; Niemann et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: An increase in Oil Red O staining was seen in the aberrant HFs of Mettl3 cKO skin, consistent with diminished WNT signaling.
source: Consistent with diminished WNT signaling in the Mettl3 cKO skin, an increase in Oil Red O staining was seen in the aberrant HFs (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by Oil Red O staining data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The paucity of lipids in the P6 dermis was expected due to the failure to suckle and weight loss likely caused by the tongue defects.
source: The paucity of lipids in the P6 dermis was expected due to the failure to suckle and weight loss likely caused by the tongue defects.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed tongue defects and weight loss.

claim: The Mettl3 cKO phenotypes bore a striking resemblance to the mice expressing a dominant negative form of LEF1 in their skin epithelium.
source: These phenotypes bore a striking resemblance to the mice expressing a dominant negative form of LEF1 in their skin epithelium.
evidence: This is a comparison to prior literature on LEF1 mutant mice.

claim: By the 15th day post-engraftment, whereas control skin had generated a thick hair coat, the cKO skin showed a striking paucity of hair growth.
source: To interrogate the long-term consequences of epidermal m6A depletion, we engrafted the back skin of P0 control and cKO littermates onto Nude mice. By the 15th day post-engraftment, the epithelium of both control and cKO skins were YFP+, indicating that they had survived the engraftment procedure (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). However, whereas control skin had generated a thick hair coat, the cKO skin showed a striking paucity of hair growth (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This is supported by engraftment data shown in Figure 3F,G.

claim: Oil Red O staining of engrafted skin further corroborated the P6 analyses and suggested that cKO progenitors follow the sebocyte versus HF path of morphogenesis.
source: Oil Red O staining further corroborated our P6 analyses and suggested that cKO progenitors follow the sebocyte versus HF path of morphogenesis (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by Oil Red O staining data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Ultrastructural analysis confirmed the arrested growth of HFs and the presence of Mettl3 null HFs that failed to engulf the DP.
source: Many of these features were confirmed at the ultrastructural level, including the arrested growth of HFs and the presence of Mettl3 null HFs that failed to engulf the DP (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Morphological signs of apoptosis were seen in P0 HFs, which were substantiated by activated (cleaved) Caspase-3 and TUNEL staining.
source: Although we did not see gross signs of junctional defects, we did see morphological signs of apoptosis in P0 HFs, which we substantiated by activated (cleaved) Caspase-3 and TUNEL staining (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that the defects went beyond mere signaling perturbations.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the hair placodes that did initiate, spindle orientations appeared to be largely unaltered and remained perpendicular to the underlying basement membrane.
source: Moreover, the organization of HF cells also appeared to be perturbed. In the hair placodes that did initiate, spindle orientations appeared to be largely unaltered and remained perpendicular to the underlying basement membrane (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by spindle orientation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Apical cytoskeletal polarization of progenitors facing the DP appeared to be perturbed in Mettl3 cKO HFs.
source: However, as judged by phalloidin staining to visualize F-actin, apical cytoskeletal polarization of progenitors facing the DP appeared to be perturbed (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by phalloidin staining data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In contrast to control skin, cKO hair placodes/germs were left behind in the dermal fraction after dispase treatment as early as E17.5.
source: We first tried dispase treatment to enrich for in vivo skin epithelium, but in contrast to control skin, cKO hair placodes/germs were left behind in the dermal fraction as early as E17.5 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Despite the ability of cKO skin progenitors to survive in vivo until birth, Mettl3 null skin epithelial progenitors failed to form colonies in vitro.
source: When we turned to in vitro culture, we learned that despite the ability of cKO skin progenitors to survive in vivo until birth, Mettl3 null skin epithelial progenitors failed to form colonies (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: High-quality sequencing data were obtained from 4443 control cells and 3455 Mettl3 null cells for scRNA-seq.
source: We then processed these isolated cells through the 10X Genomics Next GEM system for scRNA-seq, from which we obtained high-quality sequencing data from 4443 control cells and 3455 Mettl3 null cells.
evidence: This is a description of the scRNA-seq experimental data.

claim: Unbiased clustering of the cells based on their gene expression profiles indicated seven major clusters.
source: Unbiased clustering of the cells based on their gene expression profiles indicated seven major clusters as revealed by t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) plots whose identities were ascertained based upon established markers (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data and clustering analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Three clusters were related to basal epidermal progenitors (Epi basal) and were typified by high Krt5 and Krt14 expression.
source: Three clusters were related to basal epidermal progenitors (Epi basal) and were typified by high Krt5 and Krt14 expression.
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data and marker gene expression analysis.

claim: One cluster was classified as the differentiating suprabasal epidermal keratinocytes (Epi suprabasal), based upon their high Krt1 and Krt10 expression.
source: We classified one cluster as the differentiating suprabasal epidermal keratinocytes (Epi suprabasal), based upon their high Krt1 and Krt10 expression.
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data and marker gene expression analysis.

claim: The cluster with elevated expression of Shh, Lef1 and Ctnnb1 was identified as the WNThi cells of specified HFs.
source: The cluster with elevated expression of Shh, Lef1 and Ctnnb1 (encoding WNT-activated β-catenin) was identified as the WNThi cells of specified HFs, while the two clusters with high expression of Krt17 and Sox9 and little or no Lef1 were typical of WNTlo cells.
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data and marker gene expression analysis.

claim: The two clusters with high expression of Krt17 and Sox9 and little or no Lef1 were typical of WNTlo cells.
source: The cluster with elevated expression of Shh, Lef1 and Ctnnb1 (encoding WNT-activated β-catenin) was identified as the WNThi cells of specified HFs, while the two clusters with high expression of Krt17 and Sox9 and little or no Lef1 were typical of WNTlo cells.
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data and marker gene expression analysis.

claim: For control skin, most of the cells fell along two main branches: a hair germ branch composed largely of WNThi and WNTlo cells; and an interfollicular epidermal branch of basal progenitors and their suprabasal progeny.
source: To assess lineage differentiation trajectories, we performed pseudotime analyses on both control and cKO transcriptomes (Figure 5C). As expected, for control skin, most of the cells fell along two main branches: a hair germ branch composed largely of WNThi (Krt17+Lhx2+Sox9neg) and WNTlo (Krt17+Sox9+Tgfbr2+) cells; and an interfollicular epidermal branch of Krt5hiKrt14hi basal progenitors and their suprabasal Krt1+Krt10+ progeny.
evidence: This is supported by pseudotime analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The population of WNThi cells along the HF branch was markedly diminished in the cKO.
source: In agreement with the phenotypic abnormalities, the population of WNThi cells along the HF branch was markedly diminished in the cKO, and some WNThi cells were abnormally positioned along an extra lineage branch.
evidence: This is supported by pseudotime analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: 2555 genes were downregulated with a cut-off Z score of <−1.96 upon METTL3 loss.
source: Although the dynamic range of fold changes for this RNA cohort was low, 2555 genes were downregulated with a cut-off Z score of <−1.96 (all dots on the left of the dotted line in the plots of Figure 6A; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Many of the downregulated mRNAs fell into signaling pathways that had surfaced when a correlation between high m6A with efficient translation was discovered.
source: Intriguingly, many of these mRNAs fell into signaling pathways that had surfaced when we discovered a correlation between high m6A with efficient translation (Figure 6B; compare with Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of scRNA-seq data with miCLIP and ribosomal profiling data.

claim: Some of the most significantly downregulated mRNAs upon Mettl3 ablation were ones that were amongst the most highly m6A-modified in wild-type cells.
source: Moreover, although the mRNAs within these categories differed, some of the most significantly downregulated mRNAs upon Mettl3 ablation were ones that were amongst the most highly m6A-modified in wild-type cells (blue dots in Figure 6A; blue-highlighted mRNAs in Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by integrated analysis of miCLIP and scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Canonical translation initiation complex factors were among the cohort of significantly downregulated mRNAs upon METTL3 loss.
source: Of additional note, canonical translation initiation complex factors were also included in the cohort of significantly downregulated mRNAs, suggesting an additional layer of effects on global translation through m6A.
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Lef1 mRNA was significantly downregulated in both basal epidermal and WNThi progenitors upon METTL3 loss.
source: Although Lef1 was not within the top 20% of m6A-modified mRNAs, it was within the top cohort of significantly downregulated mRNAs upon Mettl3 targeting and was confirmed by quantitative PCR (qPCR) (Figure 6C). Lef1 mRNAs were reduced in both basal epidermal and WNThi progenitors, further suggesting that some basal epidermal progenitors were unable to progress to form HFs without m6A modification.
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data and qPCR validation shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Both Jag1 and Maml2 were among the most highly m6A-modified mRNAs and among the most significantly downregulated upon METTL3 loss.
source: It was also notable that the NOTCH signaling pathway also resurfaced in our loss of function analyses of basal epidermal progenitors. Both Jag1 and Maml2 were among the most highly m6A-modified mRNAs and among the most significantly downregulated (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by integrated analysis of miCLIP and scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: HES1 was diminished in Mettl3 cKO skin.
source: NOTCH signaling functions suprabasally at the transition between the basal and spinous layer, where it is typified by expression of classical NOTCH target, HES1 (Blanpain et al., 2006). Indeed, as judged by whole-mount immunofluorescence, HES1 was diminished (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Components of hemidesmosomes, for example BPAG1 (Col17A1) and integrin β4 (Itgb4), were among the most significantly downregulated mRNAs upon METTL3 loss.
source: We were particularly intrigued by this latter possibility since components of hemidesmosomes, for example BPAG1 (Col17A1) and integrin β4 (Itgb4), which are responsible for the bulk of basal cell adhesion to the basement membrane (Dowling et al., 1996), were among the most significantly downregulated mRNAs upon METTL3 loss (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 6B and a citation to prior literature.

claim: The percentage of EdU-suprabasal:BrdU-basal cells was greater in the cKO skin, indicating that Mettl3 null basal progenitors fluxed at a higher rate than normal into the suprabasal layers.
source: We therefore performed a pulse-chase experiment, by first administering a short pulse of deoxythymidine analog 5-ethynyl-2′-deoxyuridine (EdU) on E18.5 pups, and then treating with bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU) just prior to analyses (Figure 6E). Although labeling was somewhat higher in the basal cells of cKO compared to control skin, BrdU incorporation was limited to the basal progenitors in both. Most notably, the percentage of EdU-suprabasal:BrdU-basal cells was greater in the cKO skin, indicating that Mettl3 null basal progenitors fluxed at a higher rate than normal into the suprabasal layers.
evidence: This is supported by EdU/BrdU pulse-chase data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The PCAD:ECAD ratio was significantly lower than normal in Mettl3 cKO skin.
source: Additional signs of basal:suprabasal perturbations in the epidermis were revealed by immunofluorescence imaging for the basal progenitor cadherin, P-cadherin (PCAD), relative to E-cadherin (ECAD), a pan-epidermal marker. While fluorescence intensities showed that both cadherins were elevated at intercellular borders, the PCAD:ECAD ratio was significantly lower than normal (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The spindle orientations of Mettl3 null cell divisions were largely unaltered and remained within the plane of the basal layer.
source: The spindle orientations of Mettl3 null cell divisions were largely unaltered and remained within the plane of the basal layer (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by spindle orientation analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: At P0, a 45 min pulse with EdU revealed signs of elevated proliferation in the cKO basal cells.
source: However, at P0, a 45 min pulse with EdU revealed signs of elevated proliferation in the cKO basal cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by EdU labeling data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: There was a marked increase in cellularity, particularly within the spinous layers of Mettl3 cKO epidermis.
source: Rather, we attribute this change to reflect replacements due to the increased departure of basal cells into the suprabasal layers. This was accompanied by a marked increase in cellularity, particularly within the spinous layers (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Suprabasal cells were smaller than normal in Mettl3 cKO epidermis.
source: Suprabasal cells were also smaller than normal (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by cell size measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The four stages of terminal differentiation in Mettl3 cKO epidermis were still recognizable by morphology and by molecular markers.
source: Although the four stages of terminal differentiation in Mettl3 cKO epidermis were still recognizable by morphology and by molecular markers (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 2E), perturbations reverberated into the later stages of differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Mettl3 cKO epidermis displayed an appreciable number of nuclei in their granular layers.
source: In contrast, Mettl3 cKO epidermis displayed an appreciable number of nuclei in their granular layers (Figure 6G) and showed little or no signs of TUNEL positive cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Small gaps were often noted ultrastructurally at intercellular borders in the Mettl3 cKO epidermis.
source: Additionally, although desmosomes and hemidesmosomes were still present, small gaps were often noted ultrastructurally at intercellular borders in the Mettl3 cKO epidermis (arrow in Figure 6G, middle frame).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The skin barrier of neonatal Mettl3 cKO mice was still functional as judged by its ability to retain fluids.
source: Given the many perturbations seen in the Mettl3 null epidermis, it was remarkable that the skin barrier of neonatal mice was still functional as judged by its ability to retain fluids (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by TEWL measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: A considerable cohort of mRNAs that were heavily m6A-modified in wild-type had significantly upregulated mRNA levels upon m6A loss.
source: Interestingly, a considerable cohort surfaced whose mRNA levels were significantly upregulated upon m6A loss, and which had a higher dynamic range of fold-changes than the downregulated mRNAs (Figure 7A, red dots in the right quadrant; Supplementary file 3, 4 with a cut-off Z score >1.96).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: mRNAs that showed high m6A modifications within their coding sequences were generally more up- than downregulated upon METTL3 loss.
source: In fact, mRNAs that showed high m6A modifications within their coding sequences were generally more up- than downregulated upon METTL3 loss (Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The major enriched GO term categories of highly modified mRNAs in wild-type that were significantly upregulated upon m6A loss revealed changes in various aspects of RNA metabolism.
source: In all four populations, the major enriched GO term categories of highly modified mRNAs in wild-type that were significantly upregulated upon m6A loss revealed changes in various aspects of RNA metabolism, including RNA binding, RNA processing, RNA modification, ribosome and translation, as well as ribonucleoprotein complex (Figure 7B; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: CAP-independent translation was among the upregulated GO terms upon METTL3 loss.
source: Interestingly, CAP-independent translation was among the upregulated GO terms, consistent with the reduced mRNA levels that we had detected for canonical initiation.
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: mRNAs encoding all three of the major m6A reader proteins—Ythdf1, Ythdf2 and Ythdf3—were not only heavily m6A-modified in their coding sequences but also significantly upregulated upon m6A loss.
source: Additionally, of note, mRNAs encoding all three of the major m6A reader proteins—Ythdf1, Ythdf2 and Ythdf3 (Wang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2014a)—were not only heavily m6A-modified in their coding sequences (Supplementary file 4), but also significantly upregulated upon m6A loss (Z-scores ranging from 3.8 to 16) (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by integrated analysis of miCLIP and scRNA-seq data.

claim: Pelota (Pelo) was upregulated upon METTL3 loss.
source: The upregulation of Pelota (Pelo) was also intriguing (Figure 7C). Pelota is a component of the evolutionarily conserved quality control machinery that rescues stalled ribosomes, and it is also essential for skin epidermal integrity (Liakath-Ali et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 7C and a citation to prior literature.

claim: Both Myc and Bmyc mRNAs were highly modified by m6A within their coding sequences and were significantly elevated within the Mettl3 null epidermal progenitors of E17 skin.
source: In this regard, it is also noteworthy that both Myc and Bmyc mRNAs were not only highly modified by m6A within their coding sequences, but also by scRNA-seq, were significantly elevated within the Mettl3 null epidermal progenitors of E17 skin (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by integrated analysis of miCLIP and scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: MYC overexpression in embryonic epidermal progenitors is known to favor epidermal and sebocyte differentiation at the expense of the HF lineage.
source: Of additional note, MYC has long been linked to ribosomal biogenesis and translational control (Piazzi et al., 2019; van Riggelen et al., 2010), and MYC overexpression in embryonic epidermal progenitors is also known to favor epidermal and sebocyte differentiation at the expense of the HF lineage (Berta et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Upregulation of RNA processing factors has been observed in the skin progenitors of both MYC-overexpressing skin and Mettl3 cKO skin.
source: Notably, upregulation of RNA processing factors has been observed in the skin progenitors of both MYC-overexpressing skin (Arnold and Watt, 2001; Frye et al., 2003), and Mettl3 cKO skin.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of scRNA-seq data with prior literature.

claim: By having a cohort of key regulatory mRNAs that are heavily modified by m6A, progenitors are able to sense when the modification is lost and respond by rapidly enhancing their mRNA pool and calling into action rapid responses and rescue pathways.
source: Thus by having a cohort of key regulatory mRNAs that are heavily modified by m6A, progenitors are able to sense when the modification is lost and respond by rapidly enhancing their mRNA pool and calling into action rapid responses and rescue pathways to control the damage involved.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed upregulation of RNA metabolism factors upon m6A loss.
